name: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)

lead: Conjugated linoleic acids are a family of fatty acids found mainly in meat and dairy from ruminants such as cattle and sheep. Supplements are sold for fat loss and as a bodybuilding aid.

The interest started with mouse experiments in the late 1990s that reported large drops in body fat. Human trials have generally shown much smaller effects, and Wikipedia cites a 2012 meta-analysis finding no long-term effect on body composition in overweight or obese people.

paras: In rodents, the t10,c12 isomer was linked to body-composition changes and increased activity of carnitine palmitoyltransferase, an enzyme involved in moving fat into mitochondria for burning. The c9,t11 isomer is the main form in food and appears to have different biological effects. How well these mechanisms carry over to humans is unresolved.

Wikipedia cites a 2018 meta-analysis of randomised trials reporting that CLA supplementation may raise C-reactive protein and TNF-alpha. The US FDA categorised CLA as generally recognised as safe for use in foods in 2008. Supplement quality, isomer mix and long-term effects in humans remain areas of ongoing research.

lead: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) refers to a group of positional and geometric isomers of linoleic acid whose double bonds are conjugated. The most abundant forms are cis-9,trans-11 (rumenic acid) and trans-10,cis-12. They occur naturally in the meat and dairy fat of ruminants, produced by rumen microbes. [1][2]

CLA became a weight-management supplement after a 1997 mouse study reported 57 to 60 percent lower body fat in animals fed a CLA-supplemented diet. [3] A later mouse study attributed the body-composition changes to the trans-10,cis-12 isomer. [4]

Human trials have been less dramatic. Wikipedia reports that a 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis found no long-term effect on body composition in overweight or obese people, and that a 2018 meta-analysis found CLA supplementation may increase inflammatory markers. [1]
infobox: Family of polyunsaturated fatty acid isomers [1]
Meat and dairy from ruminants, especially grass-fed animals [1]

paras: About 28 isomers are possible in principle. In CLA the two double bonds are separated by a single bond rather than the usual two, and isomers differ in position and cis/trans geometry. [1] Ruminant microbes create CLA and its precursor trans-vaccenic acid, and tissues including the mammary gland can convert vaccenic acid to c9,t11-CLA through the enzyme delta-9 desaturase, as shown in dairy cows. [1][5]

Meat and milk from grass-fed ruminants contain more CLA than those from grain-fed animals. [1] Reviews of milk-fat synthesis describe how some diets alter rumen biohydrogenation and reduce milk fat, with the trans-10,cis-12 isomer implicated. [6]

The isomers have distinct effects. Reviews of the biologically active isomers describe c9,t11 as the principal dietary form and attribute lipid and body-composition effects in animals mainly to t10,c12. [2][4][7]

Animal studies have also examined effects on glucose tolerance in diabetic rats and on atherosclerosis in rabbits. [8][9] Wikipedia notes that insulin-related effects in diabetic rats have not been shown in humans. [1]

Several small human trials have been registered, including studies of CLA on body fat in overweight children (NCT00575991, 62 participants), body weight and fat oxidation in obese people (NCT00204932, 53 participants), obese women (NCT02529046) and adults with a BMI of 25 or above (NCT04641494, 58 participants). [10][11][12][13] Other registered trials have tested CLA in type 2 diabetes, asthma, breast cancer tissue and advanced solid tumours. [14][15]

Wikipedia summarises the evidence as follows: a 2015 review found no conclusive evidence of benefit for human health, a 2012 meta-analysis found no long-term body-composition effect in overweight or obese people, and a 2018 meta-analysis of randomised trials reported increases in the inflammatory markers CRP and TNF-alpha. [1]

The US FDA classed CLA as generally recognised as safe for use in foods in 2008. The US and Codex Alimentarius exempt conjugated trans bonds from trans-fat labelling rules. [1] A 2002 study cited by Wikipedia linked isomer-dependent oxidative stress and raised CRP to CLA supplementation. [1]

Research continues on individual isomers, their roles in lipid metabolism and the effect of dietary versus supplement sources. Wikipedia notes that research on its biological activity began after a 1979 finding that CLA inhibited chemically induced cancer in mice. [1]
